Three issues:
1. Line ~2224-2227: normal link-down should not jump to `rearm`; upper layer condition has `ret == OK && !up`, so once link up then cable disconnected, either `priv->carrier = false` and `netdev_lower_carrier_off()`, the interface remains RUNNING; on reconnect, `report = !priv->carrier` doesn't generate a new carrier-on notification. Should only return to rearm for negotiation branches, let the confirmed link-down go through state update and notification path, and verify up→down→reconnect.

2. Line ~1406-1409: Before publishing OWN, need RX DMA buffer cache sync. netpkt_alloc() then directly submit DMA address, only gm_desc_sync() flushes descriptor, doesn't handle the possibly dirty cache lines in the packet data region. Reusing the IO buffer, CPU may overwrite DMA-received data with stale cache lines. The file explicitly permits data buffer sharing with IOB meta non-opposite-direction, ARM64 up_invalidate_dcache() does clean-and-invalidate on this range... the "cache maintenance" on receive.

3. Line ~2143-2154: Unconfirmed bidirectional DMA stop shouldn't continue releasing the ring. Only RX's RPS checked, no TX stop check, and timeout exhaustion goes the same path as success — gm_ifdown subsequently unconditionally gm_rings_free(), releasing RX/TX packet and descriptor. Streaming mid-ifdown or stop timeout, hardware may still access these freed/reused memory. Let the stop function return inspectable result, confirm both RX/TX stopped; on failure use a reset/isolation path that can prove DMA stopped, and keep memory until then.

103:  */

115: /* One descriptor per D-cache line.
116:  *
117:  * The descriptor itself is 16 bytes, so four of them share a 64-byte cache
118:  * line.  The cache maintenance in gm_desc_sync()/gm_desc_inval() works on
119:  * lines, not on 16-byte objects: writing descriptor N+1 dirties the line that
120:  * also holds descriptor N, and the clean that follows writes the whole line
121:  * back -- including the cached copy of N's OWN bit.  If the DMA completed N
122:  * before that clean, the clean puts OWN=1 back, the DMA never revisits the
123:  * descriptor because it is behind the tail, and gm_tx_reap() waits for a
124:  * completion that can never come: the TX ring fills and every transmit
125:  * returns -ENOMEM.  That is a rare race at a steady 130 Mbit/s (it needs N's
126:  * completion to land between the two descriptor writes) and an immediate one
127:  * when a large send buffer makes the stack queue several descriptors back to
128:  * back.
129:  *
130:  * The fix is to give each descriptor its own line and tell the DMA to skip
131:  * the padding: DMA_CH0_CONTROL.DSL inserts that skip between descriptors.
132:  * The DWC units the skip by its data bus width, and the TRM gives this GMAC
133:  * a 64-bit application-side interface, so the unit is a dword (8 bytes) and
134:  * (64 - 16) / 8 = 6.  Descriptor n then lives at base + 64n and a cache
135:  * operation on it can only touch its own line.
136:  *
137:  * The earlier attempt at padding without DSL is what produced the "sends one
138:  * frame and reports transmit buffer unavailable" symptom recorded in the
139:  * memory notes: with DSL left at zero the DMA walked base, base+16, base+32
140:  * and stopped in the padding.
141:  */
142: 
143: #define GM_DESC_SIZE   16
144: #define GM_DESC_STRIDE 64
145: #define GM_DESC_DSL    ((GM_DESC_STRIDE - GM_DESC_SIZE) / 8)
146: #define GM_TX_DESC     CONFIG_RK3576_GMAC_TX_DESC
147: #define GM_RX_DESC     CONFIG_RK3576_GMAC_RX_DESC
148: 
149: /* Quota is what netpkt_alloc()/netpkt_get() will hand out for a direction.
150:  *
151:  * The transmit quota is one less than the ring depth.  The ring tells "full"
152:  * from "empty" by keeping one slot unused (next == txdone means full), so
153:  * only depth - 1 packets can be in flight.  Giving the stack the full depth
154:  * lets it offer one more than the ring can take: the driver answers -ENOMEM,
155:  * and the upper half drops that packet *after* the TCP send state has moved
156:  * past it, so only an RTO recovers it.  With the default 32 KiB send buffer
157:  * the stack rarely manages a burst that fills the ring and the bug is rare;
158:  * with 64 KiB it fills the ring in the first poll and the connection settles
159:  * into one dropped segment per retransmission timeout -- a trickle at
160:  * 0.2 Mbit/s instead of a gigabit.
161:  *
162:  * The receive quota has to be larger than the ring, because a completed frame
163:  * is replaced *before* it is handed up: receive() allocates the buffer for the
164:  * descriptor's next use while the received packet is still held here, and the
165:  * framework only returns that packet's quota after receive() has returned. Set

167:  * every received frame is dropped on the floor with no error anywhere -- the

169:  * pending-queue path, and IP never sees a packet.  Other drivers spell this as
170:  * "ring depth + spare" for the same reason (e1000's E1000_RX_QUOTA).
171:  */

/****************************************************************************
 * RK3576 Gigabit Ethernet MAC (DWC EQOS) driver.
 *
 * The driver owns everything that belongs to the controller: the CRU clocks,
 * the SDGMAC_GRF RGMII mode registers, the VCCIO RGMII delay lines, the MDIO
 * bus and the PHY state machine, the descriptor rings, and the netdev lower
 * half.  What it does *not* own is what belongs to the board: which pins carry
 * the RGMII signals, and the PHY reset line.  Those come in through the
 * configuration structure below, which the board layer fills in.
 *
 * Two instances, one file, from the first line: GMAC0 and GMAC1 are separate
 * controllers with separate MDIO buses, and nothing but the CRU gate register
 * and the clock tree is shared.
 ****************************************************************************/

#ifndef __VENDOR_ROCKCHIP_CHIPS_RK3576_RK3576_GMAC_H
#define __VENDOR_ROCKCHIP_CHIPS_RK3576_RK3576_GMAC_H

/****************************************************************************
 * Included Files
 ****************************************************************************/

#include <nuttx/config.h>

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdint.h>

#include <nuttx/net/mii.h>

#ifdef CONFIG_RK3576_GMAC

/* Controller instance indices, used as the first argument of
 * rk3576_gmac_initialize().  They index the CRU clock names, the base
 * addresses, the interrupt numbers and the SDGMAC_GRF/VCCIO registers, so
 * they are the controller index and not the port number.
 */

#define RK3576_GMAC0 0
#define RK3576_GMAC1 1

/****************************************************************************
 * Public Types
 ****************************************************************************/

/* Everything the driver needs to know about the board's port.
 *
 * The RGMII delay taps are board facts that cannot be discovered at run time
 * -- they come from the vendor DTB -- so they are passed in rather than probed
 * and guessed.  The callbacks are the board's half of the bring-up.
 */

struct rk3576_gmac_config_s
{
  /* RGMII delay lines, in 1/8 ns taps.  VCCIO_IOC MISC_CON offset differs
   * per controller *and* per pin group; the board passes the offset of the
   * group it actually muxed.
   */

  uint16_t ioc_offset;
  uint8_t tx_delay;
  uint8_t rx_delay;
  bool tx_delay_ena;
  bool rx_delay_ena;

  /* The port's own MAC address.  Nothing on this board supplies one -- no
   * DTB property, no OTP -- so it is a board decision and it must be in
   * place before the interface is brought up.
   */

  FAR const uint8_t *mac;

  /* The PHY on this port, described the way NuttX describes one: identity,
   * the address range to look in, and -- for parts that have one -- the
   * vendor status register and how to decode it.  See struct phy_desc_s in
   * <nuttx/net/mii.h>, and imx9_enet's BOARD_ENETn_PHY_LIST for the same use.
   *
   * Two fields carry meaning that header does not spell out, and both are
   * used by this board:
   *
   *   id1 == 0 && id2 == 0   the part has no PHY ID registers, so it is
   *                          identified by its status register alone (the
   *                          MAE0621A's register map has no 2 or 3)
   *   status == 0xffff       the part has no vendor status register, so
   *                          clause 22's own registers are read instead
   */

  FAR const struct phy_desc_s *phy;

  /* The board's PHY driver, or NULL for a port that only needs clause 22.
   *
   * `phy_init` configures the part after it has been reset and before
   * autonegotiation starts; `phy_advertise` writes what it can do, before this
   * driver restarts autonegotiation.  `phy_ctx` is whatever the board passed,
   * and is handed back unchanged.
   *
   * These are plain `void *` on purpose: the PHY driver lives in the drivers
   * tree, this header is in the chip tree, and neither includes the other. The
   * board is the only place that sees both, and it is what joins them up.  The
   * PHY interface's own note says the same from its side.
   */

  CODE int (*phy_init)(FAR void *ctx);
  CODE int (*phy_advertise)(FAR void *ctx);
  FAR void *phy_ctx;

  /* Board callbacks.  Both are required: without the pads muxed and the PHY
   * out of reset, nothing below works.
   *
   *   pinmux     mux the RGMII pad group (idempotent: called at boot and on
   *              every ifup)
   *   phy_reset  drive PHYRSTB, true = hold in reset, false = release
   */

  CODE int (*pinmux)(void);
  CODE void (*phy_reset)(bool assert);
};

/****************************************************************************
 * Public Function Prototypes
 ****************************************************************************/

/****************************************************************************
 * Name: rk3576_gmac_initialize
 *
 * Description:
 *   Bring the platform layer up (clocks, SDGMAC_GRF, RGMII delays, controller
 *   reset), verify that the controller answers, probe the PHY over MDIO, and
 *   register the netdev -- but do not start the DMA rings.  Those come up in
 *   ifup, on the thread that runs `ifup eth0`.
 *
 *   Called once per controller, from board_late_initialize().
 *
 * Input Parameters:
 *   intf - RK3576_GMAC0 or RK3576_GMAC1
 *   cfg  - board description of this port (see above).  The driver keeps the
 *          pointer, so the structure must stay valid for the life of the
 *          port: a `static const` in the board file is what it is for.
 *
 * Returned Value:
 *   OK on success, a negated errno on failure.
 *
 ****************************************************************************/

int rk3576_gmac_initialize(int intf,
                           FAR const struct rk3576_gmac_config_s *cfg);

/****************************************************************************
 * Name: rk3576_gmac_mdio_read / rk3576_gmac_mdio_write
 *
 * Description:
 *   Clause 22 access to a port's management bus.  A board-side PHY driver
 *   reaches the part through these; the board adapts them to the PHY
 *   interface's callbacks, which is what keeps the two trees from including
 *   each other.  `intf` is RK3576_GMAC0 or RK3576_GMAC1.
 *
 * Returned Value:
 *   Zero on success, a negated errno on failure; -ENODEV while the port has
 *   not been registered.
 *
 ****************************************************************************/

int rk3576_gmac_mdio_read(int intf, uint8_t phyaddr, uint8_t regaddr,
                          FAR uint16_t *value);
int rk3576_gmac_mdio_write(int intf, uint8_t phyaddr, uint8_t regaddr,
                           uint16_t value);

#endif /* CONFIG_RK3576_GMAC */
#endif /* __VENDOR_ROCKCHIP_CHIPS_RK3576_RK3576_GMAC_H */

234: | `pclk_sdgmac_root` | [9:8] CPLL/10, CPLL/20, 24 M | — | `GATE_CON42[2]` | `rk3576_clk_register_apb` |
235: | `aclk_sdgmac_root` | [7] GPLL, CPLL | [6:2], reset 3 (/4) | `GATE_CON42[1]` | `rk3576_clk_register_axi` |
236: 
237: Where each root *lives* follows the file's rule for every other bus domain, not
238: the SDGMAC name: `aclk_*_root` goes in the AXI function, `pclk_*_root` in the
239: APB one, `hclk_*_root` in the AHB one — exactly the way `aclk_nvm_root` and
240: `hclk_nvm_root` are already split. The VO0/VI/VEPU clusters are the exception
241: (all three roots in the peripheral's own function) and are **not** the model
242: here. `rk3576_clk_register_gmac()` therefore holds only the SDGMAC *leaves*
243: (`pclk_sdgmac_grf`, `aclk/pclk_gmac0/1`) plus the MAC/PTP clocks.
244: 
245: `aclk_gmac0/1` hang off `aclk_sdgmac_root` and `pclk_gmac0/1` off
246: `pclk_sdgmac_root`, so the roots must be registered (not just the leaf gates)
247: or the gates have no parent. `pclk_sdgmac_grf` (the SDGMAC_GRF register-file
248: clock needed to write `GMACn_CON`) also hangs off `pclk_sdgmac_root`.
249: 
250: ### The 125 MHz functional clock — divider-only off CPLL
251: 
252: | clock | gate | divider |
253: | --- | --- | --- |
254: | `clk_gmac0_125m_src` | `GATE_CON03` (0x080C) [6] | `CLKSEL_CON30` (0x0378) [14:10], reset 0x07 |
255: | `clk_gmac1_125m_src` | `GATE_CON03` [7] | `CLKSEL_CON31` (0x037C) [4:0], reset 0x07 |
256: 
257: The TRM field name is `clk_matrix_gmac<n>_125m_src_div`, but the register
258: describes **only** a divider — there is no parent mux, which is why this was
259: previously flagged as single-source. Mainline `clk-rk3576.c` supplies what the
260: TRM omits: both are `COMPOSITE_NOMUX` clocks off **`cpll`**. So the source is
261: not in doubt; only the rate is, because the reset divider of 7 (/8) gives
262: 125 MHz **only if CPLL is 1 GHz**. Treat the divider as rate-dependent and have
263: the driver call `clk_set_rate(clk_gmac<n>_125m_src, 125000000)` rather than
264: trust the reset value.
265: 
266: The divider deliberately does **not** carry `CLK_SET_RATE_PARENT`: CPLL is
267: shared with the rest of the SoC, so a rate request must be satisfied by the
268: divider alone. The gate above it does carry the flag, which is how
269: `clk_set_rate()` reaches the divider. Note the `beacon` driver's `clk_gmac<n>_en`
270: with a settable rate does not correspond to anything in the CRU.
271: 
272: ### The 25 MHz PHY reference — crystals, and NC resistors on the PHY clock
273: 
274: `refclko25m_gmac0/1_out`: mux+div in `CLKSEL_CON36` (0x0390) [7]+[6:0] and
275: [15]+[14:8]; gates in `GATE_CON05` (0x0814) [10] and [11]. The DTB lists
276: `clocks = <&cru 0x31/0x32>` on the two `phy@1` nodes, which is why this had to
277: be asked about at all.
278: 
279: The schematic closes it:
280: 
281: - **Each MAE0621A has its own 25 MHz crystal**, on XTAL_IN/XTAL_OUT (pins
282:   36/37), and both are fitted. Neither PHY takes a clock from the SoC.
283: - The SoC's 25 MHz outputs are not even routed to the PHYs:
284:   `ETH0_CLK0_25M_OUT_M0` is `GPIO3_A4`, which the board uses as `IRC_BIN` (IR
285:   receiver; the vendor DTB also claims it in its `gpio-leds` node, default
286:   off), and `GPIO2_D6` is not connected to PHY1. So `CLKSEL_CON36` /
287:   `GATE_CON05` stay untouched, and the DTB's `clocks = <&cru 0x31/0x32>` on
288:   `phy@1` is inert here.
289: - The PHY's own `CLKOUT` (pin 35, 125/25 MHz) runs to `GMACn_MCLKINOUT_M0` —
290:   `GPIO3_B0` for gmac0, `GPIO2_D7` for gmac1 — **through R1901/R1902, both
291:   marked NC and unpopulated**: the net exists, but it is not connected to the
292:   SoC pin. That is what makes `clock_in_out = "output"` a fact rather than an
293:   option — the MAC cannot take its 125 MHz from the PHY and must generate it
294:   from CPLL (see "The 125 MHz functional clock" above). If those resistors are
295:   ever fitted, this section and that one both change.
296: 
297: If a future revision drops the crystals, wiring up `refclko25m` is the first
298: thing to do: forgetting it looks exactly like a dead controller.
299: 
300: ### What the driver must request from the clock tree
301: 
302: The vendor DTB's `clock-names` on `ethernet@2a220000/2a230000` map onto the
303: registered clocks like this (gmac1 differs only in the index):
304: 
305: | DTB `clock-names` | clock to `clk_get()` | needed for |
306: | --- | --- | --- |
307: | `aclk_mac` | `aclk_gmac<n>` | AXI/CSR access |
308: | `pclk_mac` | `pclk_gmac<n>` | APB/CSR access |
309: | `stmmaceth` | `clk_gmac<n>_125m_src` | the RGMII line clock — set 125 MHz |
310: | `ptp_ref` | `clk_gmac<n>_ptp_ref` | PTP only (non-goal; tree has it) |
311: | `clk_mac_ref` | `refclko25m_gmac<n>_out` | **unused** — PHY crystals |
312: 
313: `pclk_sdgmac_grf` has no DTB entry (mainline does not model it at all) but must
314: be ungated before `GMACn_CON` can be written.
315: 
316: Enabling a leaf is enough to raise its ancestors: NuttX `__clk_enable()`
317: recurses into `clk->parent` before enabling the clock itself, and
318: `__clk_disable()` unwinds the same way. So `clk_enable("pclk_gmac0")` also
319: enables `pclk_sdgmac_root`. That is exactly why the roots had to be registered
320: rather than left as unnamed parents — the walk-up needs a resolvable parent, and
321: an unregistered one leaves the gate hanging off `NULL` (or the orphan list).
322: `pclk_sdgmac_grf` is the one GMAC clock with no child, so it alone must be
323: enabled explicitly.
324: 
325: ### SDGMAC_GRF (0x26038000) — RGMII mode and the TX clock
326: 
327: `GMAC0_CON` @0x0020, `GMAC1_CON` @0x0024. Both are hiword-write-enable
328: registers: bits [31:16] enable the write of the corresponding bit in [15:0].
329: 
330: | bits | field |
331: | --- | --- |
332: | 0 | `gmac<n>_clk_gating_en` — memory clock gate, **active high** (0 = clock on) |
333: | 2:1 | `gmac<n>_sbd_flowctrl` |
334: | 3 | RMII mode (1 = RMII, 0 = RGMII) |
335: | 4 | gate the RMII 50 MHz clock, active high |
336: | 6:5 | TX clock divider: RGMII `10` = 2.5 MHz, `11` = 25 MHz, **other = 125 MHz** |
337: | 7 | TX clock select: **0 = from CRU**, 1 = from the IO pad |
338: 
339: There is **no register at +0x0070** — the whole `GRF_CLK_CON1` model is
340: fiction.
341: 
342: ### VCCIO_IOC (0x26046000) — the RGMII delay lines
343: 
344: The only RGMII timing knob that software owns (the PHY's is strap-only). One
345: register per controller **and per pin group**:
346: 
347: | offset | owner |
348: | --- | --- |
349: | `+0x0408` MISC_CON2 | gmac0, pin group **m0** ← the K7 uses this |
350: | `+0x040C` MISC_CON3 | gmac0, pin group m1 |
351: | `+0x0410` MISC_CON4 | gmac1, pin group **m0** ← the K7 uses this |
352: | `+0x0414` MISC_CON5 | gmac1, pin group m1 |
353: 
354: Same layout in each, and hiword-write-enable:
355: 
356: ```
357: [15]    rxclk_delay_ena
358: [14:8]  rxclk_delayline_num
359: [7]     txclk_delay_ena
360: [6:0]   txclk_delayline_num
361: ```
362: 
363: ### PHY — Maxio MAE0621A (datasheet: `mae0621a-spec.txt`)
364: 
365: - Plain clause 22. Generic BMCR/BMSR/ANAR/ANLPAR/GBCR/GBSR is enough.
366: - **PHY address = 1.** An external strap block ("PHY Address Config" on the
367:   schematic) pulls PHYAD0 up and PHYAD1/PHYAD2 down, so PHYAD[2:0] = 001 — the
368:   block's own table says 1 (default). Both PHYs are wired identically and the
369:   buses are separate, so the shared address is not a conflict. Resistors are in
370:   the strap table below.
371: - **Why the DTB's `reg = <0x00>` still works.** `PHYCR1` (page `0xA43`,
372:   register 24) bit 13 `PHYAD_0 Enable` **defaults to 1**: "a command with PHY
373:   address = 0 is valid, MDC/MDIO will respond".
374: 
375:   **Measured: the PHY answers at address 0.** Both ports logged
376:   `MAE0621A at address 0, bmsr 0x7949`, and the value is a textbook BMSR, so
377:   the read really came from the part. The vendor DTB says `reg = <0>` too.
378: 
379:   **But the first management transaction after a reset fails**, and that is
380:   what makes the address look settled when it is not. The first run tried
381:   address 1 first (the strap table's value), that attempt failed, and the scan
382:   then found the part at 0 -- so "0, not 1" was never actually established: 1
383:   simply consumed the one transaction that was going to fail. Moving the
384:   descriptor to `address_lo = 0` exposed it: the *first* attempt (now 0) failed,
385:   the scan skipped 0 because it was in range, and `ifup` reported
386:   `MAE0621A did not answer on the MDIO bus` on a board that answers perfectly.
387:   So the measurement stands for 0 and says nothing about 1. The driver now
388:   primes the engine with one throwaway read, retries each presence check three
389:   times 10 ms apart, and wraps round the whole bus from the descriptor's
390:   address without skipping it. Which addresses the part actually answers at is
391:   still open, and does not matter while 0 works.
392: - **RGMII delays are strap-only.** RXD1 = `TXDLY`, RXD0 = `RXDLY` (each adds
393:   2 ns). PHYCR1, PHYCR2 and MIICR contain no delay bits (checked). So the
394:   strap and the SoC's VCCIO lines are the *only* two delay sources, and the SoC
395:   can supply delay in **both** directions in software — which makes a wrong
396:   board strap recoverable rather than fatal.
397: - **Strap values — all six confirmed on the schematic.** Each strap net has a
398:   pull-down to GND on one side and a 4.7 kΩ pull-up to `VCCIO_PHY<n>` on the
399:   other, with exactly one of the two fitted; `NC/4.7K` marks the unfitted
400:   alternative. The fitted combination:
401: 
402:   | PHY net | strap | gmac0 pin | gmac1 pin | fitted (PHY0 / PHY1) | value |
403:   | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
404:   | `RXD0` | RXDLY | `GPIO3_B2` | `GPIO2_D1` | up 4.7K, R6726 / R6826 | 1 — add 2 ns to RXC |
405:   | `RXD1` | TXDLY | `GPIO3_B1` | `GPIO2_D2` | down 4.7K, R6728 / R6828 | 0 — no 2 ns on TXC |
406:   | `RXD2` | PLLOFF | `GPIO3_D3` | `GPIO2_C0` | up 4.7K, R6724 / R6824 | 1 — stop PLL in ALDPS |
407:   | `RXD3` | PHYAD0 | `GPIO3_D2` | `GPIO2_C1` | up 4.7K, R6734 / R6833 | 1 |
408:   | `RXC` | PHYAD1 | `GPIO3_D1` | `GPIO2_C2` | down 4.7K, R6735 / R6835 | 0 |
409:   | `RXCTL`/`RXDV` | PHYAD2 | `GPIO3_A7` | `GPIO2_D3` | down 4.7K, R6736 / R6836 | 0 |
410: 
411:   So the board gives **address 1, RX delay on, TX delay off** — exactly what
412:   `rgmii-rxid` plus a SoC-side `tx_delay` calls for, and no delay is counted
413:   twice. `PLLOFF` = 1 is inert unless software enables ALDPS, and `PHYCR1`
414:   bit 2 (ALDPS Enable) defaults to 0 — leave it alone.
415: 
416:   The SoC side cannot disturb any of it: every eth pin is muxed `bias-disable`
417:   (`pcfg-pull-none`, config cell `0x1a1`), and all six strap pins are PHY→SoC
418:   directions, so the SoC is an input at strap-sampling time.
419: - **The interrupt line is wired but unused.** `INTB/PMEB` (pin 31, open-drain)
420:   goes to `GMAC0_INT/PMEB` = `GPIO3_A2` and `GMAC1_INT/PMEB` = `GPIO2_B4`.
421:   The DTB declares no `interrupts` on `phy@1` and leaves both pins unclaimed,
422:   so Linux polls link state, and phase 3 does the same. Using the line later is
423:   cheap here: `rk3576_gpio_get()` + `go_attach` already exist.
424: - **No PHY ID.** The register map (spec §8.2) does not list registers 2 and 3
425:   (PHYID1/PHYID2). Do not identify the PHY by ID: a present PHY is one whose
426:   `BMSR` (reg 1) has bit 0 set and reads neither `0xFFFF` nor `0x0000`.
427: - Reset: assert `PHYRSTB` low for ≥10 ms, then wait ≥72 ms before touching the
428:   MDIO registers. The DTB's 20 ms/100 ms is consistent.
429: - MDIO needs a 1.5 kΩ pull-up and MDC ≤ 2.5 MHz.

431: ## Attaching to the NuttX network stack
432: 
433: Two driver frameworks are alive in this tree, and the one the GMAC uses fixes
434: the driver's shape: how many times a frame is copied, who owns the buffers,
435: what serializes the driver against the stack, and what `ifup` may do. The
436: openvela guide
437: (`docs/en/device_dev_guide/connection/network/driver/net_driver_guide.md`)
438: describes the recommended one, the lowerhalf. It is right about the design and
439: its own API listing is stale in places (the header declares
440: `FAR netpkt_t *(*receive)(...)`, the guide writes a non-pointer). Read the
441: header, not the guide.
442: 
443: | | legacy (`struct net_driver_s`) | lowerhalf (`struct netdev_lowerhalf_s`) |
444: | --- | --- | --- |
445: | register | `netdev_register()`, `net/netdev/netdev_register.c` | `netdev_lower_register()`, `drivers/net/netdev_upperhalf.c:1457` |
446: | driver supplies | `d_ifup` `d_ifdown` `d_txavail` `d_ioctl` `d_addmac` `d_rmmac` and a flat `d_buf` | `ops->ifup` `ifdown` `transmit` `receive` `ioctl` `addmac` `rmmac` `reclaim` |
447: | buffer | one flat buffer the driver allocates: `MAX_NETDEV_PKTSIZE + CONFIG_NET_GUARDSIZE` = 1516 B here | `netpkt_t` (= one `iob_s`, 1516 B) from the stack's own pool |
448: | RX | driver copies the frame into `d_buf`, sets `d_len`, calls `ipv4_input()`/`arp_input()` | driver returns a `netpkt` it filled *in place*; `netdev_lower_rxready()` asks for it |
449: | TX | stack copies into `d_buf`, then calls `d_txavail` | stack passes a `netpkt` to `transmit()`; the driver owns it until `netpkt_free()` |
450: | deferral | driver's own work queue | built in: `rxtype` = work queue or a dedicated thread |
451: | flow control | driver's own | quota per direction, `netdev_lower_txdone()` |
452: | link state | `netdev_carrier_on/off()` | `netdev_lower_carrier_on/off()` |
453: | this tree's reference | `drivers/net/skeleton.c`, `drivers/net/enc28j60.c`, and the project's own `sv6621_network.c` | `drivers/net/igb.c`, `drivers/net/e1000.c` — both real descriptor-ring NICs |
454: 
455: ### The copies are on the legacy path only
456: 
457: `devif_poll()` (`net/devif/devif_poll.c:1135`) branches on `d_buf`: when it is
458: non-NULL it copies the IOB chain into the flat buffer
459: (`iob_copyout(buf, dev->d_iob, len, -llhdrlen)`) and only then calls the
460: driver's callback; `netdev_input()` (`net/netdev/netdev_input.c:68`) copies the
461: frame back the other way, `d_buf` → `d_iob`. When `d_buf` is NULL it takes
462: `devif_iob_poll()` and the driver is handed the IOB itself. So the tradeoff this
463: plan recorded — "one copy each way, revisit later" — exists only because the
464: legacy path was chosen; on the lowerhalf path there is nothing to revisit.
465: 
466: ### The IOB *is* the DMA buffer
467: 
468: `netpkt_alloc()` (`drivers/net/netdev_upperhalf.c:1824`) returns an `iob_s` out
469: of one static array, `g_iob_buffer` (`mm/iob/iob_initialize.c:62`), and this is
470: a flat build (`CONFIG_BUILD_FLAT=y`), so `up_addrenv_va_to_pa()` is the identity
471: (`chips/rk3576/rk3576_addrenv.c:98`). `netpkt_getdata()`
472: (`netdev_upperhalf.c:1943`) returns `io_data` — the guard reserve is exactly
473: `CONFIG_NET_LL_GUARDSIZE` = 14 = the Ethernet header — and 1516 B are usable
474: from there, enough for a 1514 B frame. So an RX descriptor's buffer address is
475: `up_addrenv_va_to_pa(netpkt_getdata(...))` and the frame lands in the very
476: packet the stack will read, which is what `igb_receive()`
477: (`drivers/net/igb.c:624`) does. After the DMA, `netpkt_setdatalen(dev, pkt,
478: framelen)` takes the length *including* the 14-byte header:
479: `netpkt_setdatalen()` stores `framelen - LL_HDRLEN` and `netdev_iob_replace_l2()`
480: adds the header back (`net/netdev/netdev_iob.c:175`).
481: 
482: The buffers are ordinary cached `.bss` (`CONFIG_ARCH_DCACHE=y`). Do the cache
483: maintenance unconditionally — clean before handing a descriptor to the MAC,
484: invalidate after the MAC has written — the way VICAP does
485: (`rk3576_vicap.c`: `up_clean_dcache`/`up_invalidate_dcache`). The vendor DTB
486: marks both nodes `dma-coherent`; maintenance that was not needed only costs
487: time, whereas maintenance that was skipped is silent corruption, so the DTB
488: property is not worth trusting for correctness.
489: 
490: ### Quota is the ring depth, paid out of the IOB pool
491: 
492: `netpkt_alloc()` decrements `quota[NETPKT_TX|RX]` and `netpkt_free()` puts it
493: back, so a 32-deep RX ring holds 32 of the 64 IOBs for the life of the
494: interface. `netdev_lower_register()` rejects a quota total above `NETPKT_BUFNUM`
495: (= `CONFIG_IOB_NBUFFERS` = 64) and warns above half of it (`quota_is_valid()`,
496: `netdev_upperhalf.c:119`). 16 RX + 8 TX = 24 stays under the warning line; if
497: the port proves buffer-starved the move is to raise `CONFIG_IOB_NBUFFERS`, not
498: to shrink the stack's share.
499: 
500: The two directions are not symmetric, and both asymmetries have bitten:
501: 
502: - **RX quota must be larger than the ring** (ring + spare), because a completed
503:   frame is replaced before it is handed up.
504: - **TX quota must be one smaller than the ring**, because the ring distinguishes
505:   full from empty by keeping one slot unused.  A quota equal to the ring depth
506:   lets the stack offer one packet the driver cannot take; the driver answers
507:   `-ENOMEM`, and `netdev_upper_txpoll()` drops that packet **after** the TCP
508:   send state has advanced past it, so only an RTO recovers it.  With the default
509:   32 KiB send buffer a burst rarely fills the ring; with 64 KiB the connection
510:   drops one segment per RTO and settles at 0.2 Mbit/s.  The driver now uses
511:   `GM_TX_DESC - 1`.
512: 
513: ### There is no global network lock on the data path any more
514: 
515: `net_lock()` still exists and is still a per-CPU re-entrant mutex
516: (`net/utils/net_lock.c:56`), but nothing under `net/` takes it: the input and
517: poll paths take the **per-device** lock instead — `ipv4_input()` calls
518: `netdev_lock(dev)` (`net/devif/ipv4_input.c:601`), `devif_poll()` calls it
519: (`net/devif/devif_poll.c:1135`), and `netdev_lock()` is
520: `nxrmutex_lock(&dev->d_lock)` (`include/nuttx/net/net.h:102`). Consequences:
521: 
522: - the legacy drivers in this tree still call `net_lock()` around their deferred
523:   work (`skeleton.c`, `enc28j60.c`); it serializes them against themselves on
524:   one CPU and against nothing else, and it is a mutex, so it cannot be taken in
525:   an ISR — which is why they all defer to a work queue first;
526: - on the lowerhalf path the upper half holds `netdev_lock` across its calls to
527:   `receive()`/`transmit()` (`netdev_upper_rxpoll_work()`,
528:   `netdev_upper_txavail_work()`), so the driver needs no lock of its own there;
529: - anything that takes `netdev_lock` — `netdev_lower_carrier_on/off()` above all
530:   — must run on a thread. `igb.c` says so at its link-status interrupt and
531:   defers to `LPWORK`.
532: 
533: ### The ISR does three things
534: 
535: `netdev_lower_rxready()` (`netdev_upperhalf.c:1665`) and
536: `netdev_lower_txdone()` (`:1692`) are the only stack calls that are safe from
537: an interrupt: they queue work (or post a semaphore) and return. Reaping the TX
538: ring and `netpkt_free()`-ing the completed packets may be done there too — the
539: contract in `netdev_upperhalf.c` is that `netpkt_free()` runs under no sleeping
540: lock, and `igb_txdone()` does exactly that from the handler. What the ISR must
541: not do is call the input functions or the carrier notifier.
542: 
543: ### ifup is where the hardware comes alive, and the only place it can
544: 
545: `netdev_ifup()` is reached from `SIOCSIFFLAGS`
546: (`net/netdev/netdev_ioctl.c:1063`) — i.e. from nsh's `ifup eth0` — on a user
547: thread, and it may sleep: MDIO, clock enable, PHY reset. `d_mac` settles the
548: same way: `SIOCSIFHWADDR` "will not take effect until ifup"
549: (`netdev_ioctl.c:1117`), so the MAC address registers and the unicast filter go
550: out in `ifup`, reading `dev->d_mac`, not at registration time. Registration
551: itself only fills the struct in.
552: 
553: There is no PHY/MDIO framework in this tree to attach to: `include/nuttx/net/phy.h`
554: and `drivers/net/phy_notify.c` are a SIGIO link-notification service only. The
555: driver owns MDIO and the PHY state machine. What the stack does offer is the
556: pass-through in `net/netdev/netdev_ioctl.c:1238`: `SIOCGMIIPHY`,
557: `SIOCGMIIREG` and `SIOCSMIIREG` are handed to `d_ioctl`/`ops->ioctl` with a
558: `struct mii_ioctl_data_s *`, so `ifconfig`-style tools can read the PHY through
559: the driver if the driver answers them.
560: 
561: ### Two traps
562: 
563: - **`rxtype` and `priority` default to 0**, which is `NETDEV_RX_WORK` on
564:   `HPWORK` (`include/nuttx/wqueue.h:221`: `HPWORK` = 0, `LPWORK` = 1). The
565:   network stack must never run on the high-priority queue — `skeleton.c` says
566:   so, the reason being that a worker that suspends there hangs the system. Set
567:   `rxtype = NETDEV_RX_WORK; priority = LPWORK;` explicitly, or use
568:   `NETDEV_RX_THREAD` with a real priority.
569: - **The name is assigned in registration order.** `netdev_register()` builds
570:   `eth%d` through `find_devnum()` (`net/netdev/netdev_register.c:143`), which
571:   counts the names already registered with the same prefix, so gmac0 then gmac1
572:   gives `eth0`/`eth1` — but a port that fails to initialize shifts the other
573:   one's name. Pre-filling `d_ifname` with `"eth0"` pins the name yet is still
574:   read as a format string, and `find_devnum()` `DEBUGASSERT`s `xxx%d`; it does
575:   not detect a collision. Log `dev->netdev.d_ifname` after registering rather
576:   than assume the order.
577: 
578: ### MAC address: no source on this board
579: 
580: The vendor DTB sets no `mac-address`, no `nvmem-cells` and no
581: `local-mac-address` on either `ethernet@2a220000/2a230000` node, and the RK3576
582: GMAC has no OTP MAC. The project's only other netdev takes its address from the
583: SV6621 firmware, so there is no precedent to copy: the two ports need a policy
584: (a `Kconfig` pair, or one base address with the port index mixed in) and the
585: value must be in `d_mac` before `ifup`.

587: ### Two styles in one image — what it actually costs
588: 
589: The SV6621 stays legacy, so the two styles will coexist. Measured, not assumed:
590: 
591: - **Flash: already paid.** `netdev_upperhalf.c` is compiled for any
592:   `CONFIG_NET && CONFIG_MM_IOB` (`drivers/net/Make.defs:28`), which this
593:   firmware already is; `--gc-sections` then drops what nothing references, which
594:   is why `netdev_lower_register` is absent from today's `nuttx` ELF. The object
595:   is 5880 B of `.text` in total and a wired driver does not use the wireless,
596:   VLAN and dedicated-thread parts (~1.7 KB), so the marginal cost is about
597:   **4 KB** — against 966 lines of `skeleton.c` boilerplate written and owned by
598:   us if the legacy path is taken. No new Kconfig either: there is no
599:   `CONFIG_NETDEV_LOWERHALF`, the requirement is `CONFIG_NET`, `CONFIG_MM_IOB`
600:   and `CONFIG_NETDEV_IOCTL`, all already on.
601: - **Nothing above the netdev can tell the difference.** Registry, naming,
602:   `SIOCSIF*`, MII ioctls, stats and carrier are all per-device on both paths;
603:   the lower half's upper half installs its own `d_ifup`/`d_txavail`/`d_ioctl`
604:   wrappers and then goes through the same `netdev_register()` as the SV6621.
605:   `ifup eth0`, `ifconfig`, `renew eth0` and `arp` need no change.
606: - **The one real coupling is the IOB pool.** The SV6621 holds none: its RX ring
607:   is its own `uint8_t rx_frame[4][MAX_NETDEV_PKTSIZE]` and it calls
608:   `ipv4_input()` on that flat buffer, borrowing one IOB per packet through
609:   `netdev_input()`'s copy. A lowerhalf GMAC holds one IOB per RX descriptor for
610:   as long as the interface is up — 16 RX + 8 TX is 24 of 64 — and the same pool
611:   feeds TCP read-ahead. Two things soften it: the ring is only claimed at
612:   `ifup eth0`, so WiFi is untouched until someone brings the port up; and a
613:   legacy GMAC would borrow from the same pool per packet anyway, so the
614:   difference is *held vs borrowed*, not *uses vs doesn't*. If it bites, the
615:   counter is already the one the project learned to read: `mem: iob N free`.
616: - **The honest risk points the other way.** The legacy RX/TX path is what this
617:   board has been running for the WiFi; the lowerhalf path would be new to this
618:   firmware, so its first bugs are ours to find. The code is in-tree and
619:   exercised by `igb.c`/`e1000.c`, and its failure modes are the ordinary ones
620:   (quota, packet ownership) rather than a hand-rolled copy loop — but it is new
621:   surface, and that is what the saved boilerplate is bought with.
622: 
623: What mixing does *not* cost is contention: the legacy drivers take `net_lock()`
624: in their own deferred work, the lowerhalf path never does, and since the stack
625: takes neither, the two never wait on each other.
626: 
627: ### Recommendation
628: 
629: Use the **lowerhalf**. The plan's reason for choosing legacy was
630: controllability, and the investigation takes that away: the upper half already
631: implements what `skeleton.c` hand-rolls — RX deferral, TX polling, the TX queue,
632: quota, carrier, statistics — and does it under the per-device lock the stack
633: actually takes, while `igb.c` is a working descriptor-ring NIC written against
634: the same API, i.e. a blueprint instead of a proposal. Legacy pays a copy in each
635: direction, keeps a hand-written quota emulation, and its `net_lock()` buys no
636: exclusion from the stack on this tree.
637: 
638: The one honest cost inside the driver is that `receive()`/`transmit()` are more
639: involved than `d_buf` — the driver has to know who owns a `netpkt` and when —
640: which is a phase-4 concern, not a phase-2 one. The cost of the two styles
641: coexisting in one image is listed above, and none of it lands above the netdev.

780: ### The data path: four things that each looked like "the stack is broken"
781: 
782: The link trained before any of these was found, and every one of them produced
783: the same misleading shape -- the driver saw frames, the stack did not, and no
784: register looked wrong.  In the order they were found:
785: 
786: 1. **The RX quota has to exceed the ring depth.**  `receive()` allocates the
787:    replacement buffer *before* the frame is handed up, and the framework only
788:    returns the received packet's quota after `receive()` returns.  With
789:    `quota[NETPKT_RX] == ring depth` the replacement allocation always fails, so
790:    `receive()` returns NULL and **every frame is dropped inside the driver**.
791:    The ring stays armed, the link is up, ARP still works (its reply travels the
792:    pending-queue path) and `/proc/net/stat` shows `IPv4 Received 0000` while
793:    the driver logs the frame it just threw away.  e1000 spells the same rule as
794:    `E1000_RX_QUOTA = RX_DESC + RXSPARE`.
795: 
796: 2. **The descriptor stride is the hardware's 16 bytes.**  Padding each
797:    descriptor to a full cache line (64) was tried for tidy cache maintenance
798:    and cost exactly one frame per direction: the DMA walks `base + 16n`, found
799:    the zero padding where the next OWN bit should be, reported TBU and
800:    suspended, while the driver queued frames at `base + 64n` that it never
801:    looked at.  The proof was `DMA_CH0_CURRENT_APP_TXDESC` reading `base + 16`
802:    while our base was `base`.  Cache safety comes from clean-after-write /
803:    invalidate-before-read, not from padding.
804: 
805: 3. **Tail pointers name the descriptor just published.**  Both rings advance
806:    their tail to the descriptor that was just made valid, not to the next,
807:    still-unowned one; the TRM's TBU entry names "advance the ... Tail Pointer"
808:    as the way to resume, and pointing it at a descriptor nobody owns is what
809:    the FSM stops on.
810: 
811: 4. **`RDES3[30]` (the receive descriptor's interrupt enable) must be set.**  The
812:    TRM: "the RI bit is not set ... because of the setting of Interrupt Enable
813:    bit ... RDES3[30]".  Without it the ring silently fills -- frames land in
814:    the descriptors and no interrupt announces them -- until the DMA reaches the
815:    tail and raises RBU, which drains everything at once and then stops.  The
816:    symptom is distinctive: the first `ping` after boot receives nothing, the
817:    second delivers exactly `GM_RX_DESC - 1` frames in a burst, and nothing
818:    after that.
819: 
820: Two more that were tried and reverted: issuing **StartTx per frame** (a
821: read-modify-write that sets a bit that is already 1 is not a command at all --
822: the TRM says the Start command is only effective when the transmission is
823: stopped, and the hardware reports TBU instead of clearing StartTx), and issuing
824: **StartRx per frame** (the RBU entry only asks for a poll demand when the tail
825: pointer is not used; it reset the receive process on every packet).  Neither
826: was needed once the four items above were fixed.
827: 
828: ### Testing trap: `ping` can only be trusted once per boot
829: 
830: `apps/netutils/ping` takes its ICMP id from a **static counter**
831: (`ping_newid()` is `++g_pingid`), while the stack copies whatever id the
832: application put in the header.  Run `ping` twice in one boot and the second run
833: rejects the first run's replies -- and, because the loopback test is the board
834: pinging its own other port, it rejects its own:
835: 
836: ```
837: WARNING: Ignoring ICMP reply with ID 1.  Expected 2
838: ```
839: 
840: So: **reboot, then run exactly one `ping`** when verifying.  A second `ping` in
841: the same boot will look like a 90 % loss no matter how healthy the driver is.
842: (The board's two ports cabled together is itself a workable test: eth0 pings
843: eth1's address, and the reply comes back through the same driver.)
844: 
845: ### Root cause: the PHY was reset after its analog trims, which stops the crystal
846: 
847: **Solved.** The two ports train 1000M/Full, the analog self check passes on the
848: first attempt, and `INSR` reads `0x0020` -- bit 5, "normal operation" -- which
849: it had never done before.
850: 
851: What was wrong was the *order of two things this driver did*, not any register
852: value:
853: 
854: | when | what | result |
855: | --- | --- | --- |
856: | boot, once | PHYRSTB pulse, then MDIO probe | part answers; crystal **stopped** |
857: | ifup | the vendor's analog trim sequence (see below) | crystal **starts** |
858: | ifup (old code) | **another PHYRSTB pulse** | crystal **stopped again** |
859: 
860: Every measurement that made no sense is this one fact: with the oscillator
861: stopped the part still answers MDIO, still accepts register writes, still shows
862: all documented registers at their defaults, its bias pin (RSET, 1.13 V) still
863: reads normal -- and its autonegotiation state machine, its ADC and its copper
864: side never move, so `ANER` bit 0 stays clear, `LPA` stays 0, `INSR` stays 0 and
865: the LEDs stay dark.  The vendor kernel never gets there because it resets the
866: PHY **once, at probe**, and then only ever writes registers.
867: 
868: So: **reset the PHY once, before the trim sequence, and never again.**  The
869: driver now passes `reset = (phyaddr == NONE)` to `gm_board_power()`, so a port
870: whose PHY never answered at boot still gets a second chance, and nothing else
871: pulses PHYRSTB.
872: 
873: The trim sequence itself came from the board vendor's patched kernel
874: (`patch/kernel/rk35xx-vendor-6.1/004-add-PHY-for-MAE0621A-Q2C.patch`,
875: `maxio_mae0621a_config_init()`, PHY ID 0x7b744411): about twenty writes to
876: undocumented pages (`0xd8f`, `0xd90`, `0xd91`, `0xd92`, `0xd96`, `0xd97`,
877: `0xda0`, plus two indirect MMD accesses), then an ADC self check with up to
878: fifty reset-and-retry attempts.  The datasheet documents none of it, which is
879: why matching every documented register against the vendor kernel had found
880: nothing.
881: 
882: Two details worth keeping: the vendor's own self check is **not fatal** -- their
883: `config_init` throws its result away and their board links anyway -- and the
884: self check only passes once the reference clock is alive, so it doubles as the
885: "is the crystal running" test that no register can give.
886: 
887: Also confirmed by the same schematic sheet that settled the crystal: the board
888: populates clock **Option 1** (a 25 MHz crystal per PHY, 18 pF/16 pF), and the
889: SoC-side alternative (`GMACn_MCLKINOUT_M0` through R6710/R6713 to the PHY's
890: CLKOUT, in the `MAC <-- PHY` direction) is NC.  So `refclko25m_gmac*_out` is
891: not used by this board and the driver correctly leaves it alone.

907: `struct ethernet_phy_s *` inside, and the board -- which already includes both
908: -- assigns them.  The cost is that `ethernet_phy_init()` is a two-line
909: dispatcher rather than a typed call, which is cheaper than the alternative.
910: 
911: This is this project's convention, not NuttX's: the tree has no PHY framework,
912: so the MAC keeps the clause 22 machinery the way every other MAC driver in
913: NuttX does.  If a future part needs its link decoded from a vendor status
914: register, the next step is the fuller vtable (init, advertise *and* link), not
915: a new framework.
916: 
917: What moved out of the chip: the vendor pages, PHYCR1's never-wanted bits, the
918: forced MDI mode, and the gigabit advertisement.  What stayed: everything
919: clause 22 generic, including the `struct phy_desc_s` probe and the 1 Hz link
920: poll.
921: 
922: ### The link that will not train (open)
923: 
924: Everything on the management side is nominal and the copper side shows no
925: activity at all.  Measured, in order:
926: 
927: | what | reads | verdict |
928: | --- | --- | --- |
929: | BMSR | `0x7949` (EXTCAP, ANEGABLE, 10/100 capable, link 0) | PHY alive, no link |
930: | BMCR after our write | `0x1000` (ANENABLE, restart self-cleared, no powerdown/isolate/loopback) | our write lands, autoneg runs |
931: | ANAR | `0x01e1` | advertisement correct |
932: | ANLPAR (LPA) | `0x0000` for 30 s, against *another identical PHY* and against a known-good instrument | nothing is ever heard |
933: | PHYCR1 (page 0xA43/0x18) | `0x2118` = the datasheet's defaults: PHYAD_0 en, preamble check, jabber; **ALDPS enable 0, ALDPS PLL off 0**, manual MDI 0 | no power saving, auto crossover "on" |
934: | PHYCR2 | `0x0823`: RXC out en, CLKOUT en, CLKOUT 125 MHz | clocks are *asked* for |
935: | PHYSR (0xA43/0x1a) | `0x1000`: aneg enable set, **link 0, MDI/MDIX status 0 (MDI), ALDPS state 0** | never flips, never links |
936: | LCR (page 0xD04/0x10) | `0x6251` = defaults: LED0 10M link+act, LED1 100M, LED2 1000M | the dark LEDs mean "no link", not "no LEDs" |
937: 
938: Forcing the pairing was tried both ways with the write verified by read-back
939: (GMAC0 `phycr1 0x2218` = MDIX, GMAC1 `0x2318` = MDI, i.e. a correctly paired
940: straight cable) and still no link, still `lpa 0`.  So pairing is not it --
941: *unless* PHYCR1's manual bit does not reach the data path, which is why PHYSR
942: bit 1 is worth watching: it stayed 0 on the port that was forced to MDIX.
943: 
944: The pattern -- management interface perfect, registers all at their documented
945: defaults, advertisement correct, and yet no link pulse heard, no crossover
946: progression, no link, no LED -- is what a PHY whose *copper/analog section* is
947: not running looks like.  The two candidates are the 25 MHz reference (crystal
948: on pins 36/37) and the analog rails.  Software cannot see either: the datasheet
949: exposes no clock or PLL status bit.
950: 
951: **Falsified, and what replaced it.** The board was run with its vendor Debian
952: image, same cable, ports cabled to each other: both ports come up (`end0`/`end1`
953: `UP,RUNNING`), **ping between them works**, and their LEDs light.  So the
954: hardware, the cable, the pairing and the copper side are all fine, and the
955: crystal measures 2.4 Vpp at 25 MHz (the earlier "0 V on both pins" was a 10x
956: probe loading the oscillator -- XTAL_IN is a ~1 MOhm node, so a 10 MOhm probe
957: drags its bias to nearly zero and often stops the oscillation).
958: 
959: Three things that run then taught us, each contradicting something above:
960: 
961: | claim | what the vendor kernel showed |
962: | --- | --- |
963: | "the MAE0621A has no PHY ID registers" | `phy_id = 0x7b744411` on both buses.  It has them; the datasheet's register map just omits 2 and 3. |
964: | "the PHY answers at 0, and 1 was never verified" | Linux finds it at `stmmac-0:00`, i.e. address 0.  The strap table's 1 is wrong. |
965: | "the PHY's crossover detection does not advance" | Under Linux the same two PHYs link with the same straight cable, so it works when the part is configured the way Linux configures it. |
966: 
967: Linux's clock tree, for comparison with ours: `clk_gmac0/1_125m_src` = 125 MHz
968: enabled (ours too), `aclk_gmac*` = 297 MHz, `pclk_gmac*` = 100 MHz,
969: `aclk_sdgmac_root` = 297 MHz, `hclk_sdgmac_root` = 198 MHz, and
970: `refclko25m_gmac*_out` = 25 MHz **enabled** -- but the ethernet node's pinctrl
971: does not include the `eth_clk*_25m` group, so it reaches no pin.  Our own
972: `GMACn_CON` writes are no-ops on this board: the register already reads
973: RGMII / CRU clock / 125 MHz divider / ungated, so the SoC side matches.
974: 
975: **The SoC side is verified identical.** The vendor image's SDGMAC_GRF, read
976: through debugfs (`/sys/kernel/debug/regmap/dummy-syscon@0x...26038000/`), has
977: `GMAC0_CON = GMAC1_CON = 0x00000000` -- all-zero is the right value: RGMII (bit
978: 3 clear), TX clock from the CRU (bit 7 clear), /1 divider (bits 6:5 zero),
979: memory clock ungated (bit 0 clear).  Our driver writes exactly that, which is
980: why its GRF log line never printed (old == new).  Also worth knowing: the
981: vendor image gives the two MACs `aclk` 297 MHz, `pclk` 100 MHz, and enables
982: `refclko25m_gmac*_out` at 25 MHz even though the ethernet node's pinctrl never
983: muxes it, so it reaches no pin.
984: 
985: **Reading registers from the vendor image: `busybox devmem` for MMIO only, and
986: never `/dev/mem` any other way.**  On this image `dd if=/dev/mem` is refused
987: and mapping `/dev/mem` from a python one-liner **panics the kernel**; a
988: `busybox devmem` script that poked the MAC's MDIO registers also panicked (the
989: trace was not captured, so the cause is still open -- a write through /dev/mem
990: and `ip link set ... down` on the vendor stmmac are both candidates).  Safe so
991: far: `busybox devmem <addr> 32` reads of GRF/MAC, and the debugfs regmap dump
992: above.  What is still missing from that side is PHY register 9 (`ctrl1000`),
993: which needs an MDIO transaction, and one costs a write to the MAC's
994: MDIO_ADDRESS even to read.
995: 
996: **The one difference found so far, and it was ours.** Our gigabit
997: advertisement was wrong: `GM_PHY_ADV_1000FULL` was `1 << 11`, which in register
998: 9 is the *master/slave* bit, and the value written was `0x0c00` -- 1000BASE-T
999: *half* duplex plus "as master", with **no 1000BASE-T full duplex at all**.  The
1000: part is not 1000BASE-T half duplex capable (its own GBESR says so), so we were
1001: advertising nothing this PHY can actually do at gigabit.  Linux writes `0x0200`
1002: from GBESR.  Fixed, and the trace now also logs ANER, ctrl1000 and INSR so the
1003: next run says whether autonegotiation saw a partner at all (`ANER` bit 0 =
1004: parallel detection fault, bits 1:0 = partner autoneg able/received) and how it
1005: ended (INSR bit 3 = complete, bit 0 = error).
1006: 
1007: **Next: hardware measurement, not more driver code.**
1008: 1. `CLKOUT`, pin 35: `phycr2 = 0x0823` says enabled at 125 MHz.  Nothing there
1009:    means the crystal/PLL is not running.
1010: 2. `XTAL_IN`, pin 36: 25 MHz.  Probe CLKOUT first -- a probe can stop the
1011:    oscillator.
1012: 3. RJ45 pins 1/2 (the MDI transmit pair) while autonegotiation runs: link-pulse
1013:    bursts (a ~100 ns pulse train every ~16 ms) mean the PHY is transmitting and
1014:    the fault is on the receive/magnetics side.  Silence means the transmitter is
1015:    not running, which matches everything above.
1016: 4. Analog rails and the magnetics' centre-tap bias, from the schematic.
1017: 
1018: A mistake worth recording: the first attempt at forcing the pairing read
1019: PHYCR1 through a page switch, got `0xffff` (the first management transaction
1020: after a reset can fail -- see above), OR'd the MDI bits into it and wrote
1021: `0xffff` back.  That set ALDPS enable + ALDPS PLL off (plus TX CRS and PHYAD
1022: non-zero detect) and put the PHY into link-down power saving with the PLL
1023: stopped, which is a guaranteed no-link state.  Page reads are now validated
1024: (rejects `0xffff`/`0x0000`), retried, given 100 us after the page switch, and
1025: that register's four never-wanted bits are cleared on every write, so the
1026: damage is repaired by the next `ifup`.
1027: 
1028: ### The PHY: NuttX has a descriptor, not a framework
1029: 
1030: Settled after the first run, by reading the tree rather than deciding in the
1031: abstract. The finding, because it will come up again:
1032: 
1033: - **No PHY driver layer exists.** No `phy_dev_s`, no `mdio_bus`, no
1034:   `drivers/net/phy/`, no functions in `mii.h` (its prototype section is empty).
1035:   `<nuttx/net/phy.h>` + `drivers/net/phy_notify.c` are the SIGIO link
1036:   notification service and nothing else.
1037: - **A PHY *descriptor* does exist**: `struct phy_desc_s` in
1038:   `include/nuttx/net/mii.h` — name, id1/id2, a vendor `status` register, an
1039:   `address_lo`/`address_high` range, and the `mbps10/100/1000`, `duplex`,
1040:   `speed_mask` fields that decode that register. The board supplies it
1041:   (`BOARD_ENETn_PHY_LIST` in `boards/arm64/imx9/imx93-evk/include/board.h`)
1042:   and the MAC driver walks it (`imx9_determine_phy()`).
1043: - **Every MAC driver carries its own clause 22 code**, and the board supplies a
1044:   `<chip>_phy_boardinitialize(int intf)` hook for reset/power
1045:   (`CONFIG_IMXRT_ENET_PHYINIT` and friends). imxrt additionally keeps a
1046:   `static struct phy_desc_s g_board_phys[]`; mpfs instead blind-scans the bus
1047:   (`mpfs_phyfind()`, `PHYID1 != 0xffff` over 0..31).
1048: 
1049: So the driver follows NuttX: **clause 22 is inline in `rk3576_gmac.c`**, the
1050: part is the board's `struct phy_desc_s` (`kickpi_k7_ethernet.c`), and the two
1051: pieces of meaning that structure does not spell out are stated where they are
1052: used:
1053: 
1054: | field | value | means |
1055: | --- | --- | --- |
1056: | `id1`/`id2` | both 0 | the part has **no PHY ID registers**; identify by status register only (the MAE0621A lists no registers 2 or 3) |
1057: | `status` | `0xffff` | the part has **no vendor status register**; use clause 22's own (BMSR + the 1000BASE-T pair) |
1058: | `address_lo` | 1 | the strap block's PHYAD[2:0] = 001; `address_high = 0xffff` = this one address only |
1059: | `clause` | 22 | clause 45 is rejected with `-ENOTSUP` |
1060: 
1061: The address search is the descriptor's range first, then the rest of the bus,
1062: because the MAE0621A answers at 0 as well (PHYCR1 "PHYAD_0 Enable" defaults
1063: set) — which is also why the vendor DTB says `reg = <0>` for a PHY strapped
1064: to 1.
1065: 
1066: **An earlier attempt put clause 22 in `drivers/drivers/` as its own driver**
1067: (`ethernet_phy/` + `mae0621a/`, with a project `ethernet_phy.h`). It was
1068: removed: it duplicated `struct phy_desc_s`, it would have been the only PHY
1069: driver in the tree organised that way, and it made the chip driver depend on
1070: the project driver tree's include path. `drivers/` is back to its original
1071: state.
1072: 
1073: ### First hardware run — what it proved, and what changed because of it
1074: 
1075: The board reported:
1076: 
1077: ```
1078: gmac0: 125m clock 125000000 Hz
1079: gmac0: DMA software reset never completed
1080: ERROR: GMAC0 initialization failed: -110
1081: ```
1082: 
1083: Three things follow, and all three are now in the code:
1084: 
1085: 1. **The clock tree and the APB path are alive.** The 125 MHz divider reaches
1086:    exactly 125 MHz (open item 2 closed), and the CSR write stuck and read back
1087:    as 1 — so `PD_SDGMAC` is powered, `aclk`/`pclk` are running, and the CRU
1088:    reset polarity reading ("1 asserts") is right. A block held in reset would
1089:    have read 0 and the poll would have passed.
1090: 2. **DMA `SWR` needs a clock we do not have yet.** The TRM is explicit: SWR
1091:    "is automatically cleared after the reset operation is complete in all
1092:    DWC_ether_qos clock domains", and "it is essential that all PHY input
1093:    clocks ... are present". In RGMII that includes RXC, which the PHY drives
1094:    and which need not be running before the link has trained. **The driver no
1095:    longer uses SWR**: `gm_reset()` asserts the two per-port CRU bits
1096:    (`aresetn`, `presetn`) and verifies they released, which needs no IP clock.
1097: 3. **The GRF is now programmed before the reset**, not after: it is platform
1098:    state, and a controller reset does not touch it.
1099: 
1100: The aliveness log now reads both sides of the reset on one line —
1101: `gmac0: version 0x00003051 (0x00000000 before reset)` — so the next flash says
1102: whether the block was ever alive, rather than only that it is not now.
1103: 
1104: 
1105: The plan's `RK3576_GMAC0/1` and `RK3576_GMAC_TX_DELAY_*` are not what landed.
1106: The final split follows "board facts live in the board Kconfig":
1107: 
1108: | Symbol | Where | Meaning |
1109: | --- | --- | --- |
1110: | `CONFIG_RK3576_GMAC` | chip | compiles the driver; needs `NET && NET_ETHERNET` |
1111: | `CONFIG_RK3576_GMAC_RX_DESC` / `_TX_DESC` | chip | ring depth, default 16 / 8.  Quota is depth + 4 for RX and depth - 1 for TX (see "Quota is the ring depth") |
1112: | `CONFIG_KICKPI_K7_ETHERNET` | board | the two on-board ports; selects nothing, depends on `RK3576_GMAC && RK3576_GPIO` |
1113: | `CONFIG_KICKPI_K7_ETHERNET_PORT1` | board | default y; turning it off leaves GMAC0 only |
1114: | `CONFIG_KICKPI_K7_ETHERNET_TX_DELAY0` / `1` | board | 33 / 32 taps, the vendor DTB's numbers |
1115: | `CONFIG_KICKPI_K7_ETHERNET_MACADDR0` / `1` | board | default `02:52:4b:37:76:00` / `:01` |
1116: 
1117: Both ports are enabled in `configs/ethernet`, which is the branch's main
1118: configuration (camera half included, unchanged).
1119: 
1120: ### Two things this configuration changed about the IOB pool
1121: 
1122: `CONFIG_IOB_BUFSIZE` 1516 → **1536** and `CONFIG_IOB_NBUFFERS` 64 → **128**,
1123: both in `configs/ethernet` only.
1124: 
1125: - The buffer size because the RX descriptor points straight at the netpkt's
1126:   data area: the value programmed as RBSZ *is* `CONFIG_IOB_BUFSIZE`, so it has
1127:   to hold a full frame and be a whole AXI beat. 1516 is not a multiple of 16;
1128:   the driver `#error`s on a size that is not.
1129: - The count because 16 RX + 8 TX per port × 2 ports = 48 buffers held for the
1130:   life of the interfaces, against a warning line of 64 (`NETPKT_BUFNUM / 2`).
1131:   With 128 there are 80 left for TCP read-ahead and the SV6621.
1132: 
1133: `.bss` grew 306 KB → 407 KB; `nuttx.bin` 1.92 MB → 1.96 MB, against a 4 MB
1134: firmware slot (`nboot-release.json`, `vendor_fit_size`).
1135: 
1136: ### Where the driver departs from this plan, and why
1137: 
1138: 1. **One descriptor per cache line (64-byte stride).** Descriptors are 16
1139:    bytes, so four share a line and a clean or invalidate on one would touch
1140:    its neighbours' OWN bits. With one per line every cache operation is exact,
1141:    for 3 KB of ring space per port. The rule that makes re-reading a
1142:    not-yet-complete descriptor safe: clean the line before handing it over, so
1143:    a later invalidate can only drop a stale copy.
1144: 2. **The interrupt summary enables are written twice.** The TRM puts NIE/AIE
1145:    at bits 15/14; the DWC databook mainline stmmac was written against puts
1146:    them at 16/15. Nothing in the tree can settle that without hardware, so the
1147:    driver sets both candidate positions and acts only on the individual bits
1148:    (TIE 0, RIE 6, RBUE 7, FBE 12), which both documents agree on. If the first
1149:    flash shows link up but no packets, this is the first suspect.
1150: 3. **`DMA_SYSBUS_MODE` programs only BLEN4/8/16.** The DTB's `wr_osr_lmt=4`
1151:    and `rd_osr_lmt=8` are left at their reset values: the extracted TRM text
1152:    interleaves that field's bit rows with its neighbours', so a guess buys
1153:    nothing but a mystery.
1154: 4. **Multicast is accepted wholesale** (`MAC_PACKET_FILTER.PM`), so
1155:    `addmac`/`rmmac` succeed without touching the hash table — the frame is
1156:    already being received. The low bits of that register are one of the places
1157:    the TRM text extracts badly; PM at bit 2 is the reading that cannot break
1158:    unicast either way, and IGMP/IPv6-ND is what would show it if wrong.
1159: 5. **The soft reset uses the two per-port CRU bits only** (`aresetn` and
1160:    `presetn` for the port), not the shared `sdgmac_biu`/`sdgmac_grf` bits. The
1161:    `aresetn` pair is what the DTB's reset ids confirm; the `presetn` pair is
1162:    the TRM's reading of "when high, reset relative logic". If the controller
1163:    answers with version 0, dropping `presetn` is the first thing to try, and
1164:    the code says so.
1165: 6. **The RX path allocates a replacement buffer before handing the frame up**,
1166:    and if `netpkt_alloc()` fails it leaves the descriptor alone, stalls the
1167:    ring and re-arms it from a delayed work item. A stalled ring generates no
1168:    interrupts, so without that retry the port would go silently dead the first
1169:    time the IOB pool ran dry.
1170: 
1171: ### Still open, in the order they will bite
1172: 
1173: 1. **Is the controller powered?** `PD_SDGMAC` (memory item 1 above). The boot
1174:    log's `gmac0: version 0x…` answers it: `0x00003051` means yes, `0x00000000`
1175:    means the block is dark and no driver change helps.
1176: 2. **Is the 125 MHz clock 125 MHz?** The CRU divider is off CPLL and CPLL's
1177:    rate is whatever the bootloader left. `clk_set_rate(..., 125000000)` +
1178:    readback is logged; if the divider cannot reach it the driver says so
1179:    loudly but still registers, so the port is visible rather than absent.
1180: 3. **Does the summary-enable guess hold?** See departure 2.
1181: 4. **Do the taps train gigabit?** 33/32 from the DTB; retime by rebuild via
1182:    the two board Kconfig ints.
1183: 5. The phase 4-7 work (RX, TX, port 1, 100M/10M, `ifdown`/`ifup`) is written
1184:    but unexercised.
1185: 
1186: The next flash is the phase 1+2 verdict: `gmac0/1: version`, the SDGMAC_GRF and
1187: VCCIO readbacks, `phy addr N bmsr 0x…`, `registered as eth0/eth1`, and eMMC/SDIO
1188: still working. `ifup eth0` then adds the autonegotiation and link lines.

# ethloop — the TCP loopback test for the two wired ports

`contest2026_062_PharosTech/app/ethloop`, reached through
`apps/examples/ethloop`, enabled by `CONFIG_EXAMPLES_ETHLOOP` in
`configs/ethernet/defconfig`.  Written for the stage after both GMAC ports
train a link: a cable between them, one TCP connection across it, a rate and
an integrity result.

## The one fact that makes a single-board loopback possible

**Both ports must be in the same IPv4 subnet, and the connecting socket must
be bound to the first port with `SO_BINDTODEVICE`.**

A TCP segment is transmitted on the interface the destination address routes
to, and `arp_out()` only ARPs for destinations on that interface's own
subnet.  With `eth0 = 192.168.1.1/24` and `eth1 = 192.168.2.1/24`, a segment
for `192.168.2.1` is transmitted out **eth1**, crosses the cable and arrives
on **eth0**, which drops it because the destination is not its address.  The
connection times out with no error anywhere.  No amount of driver debugging
finds this, because the driver is fine.

With both in one subnet (`192.168.77.1/24` and `.2/24`) and the client bound
to `eth0`, the segment goes out `eth0` and arrives on `eth1`, whose address it
is.  The pieces, in NuttX:

| step | function | why it lands where it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| client device | `tcp_bind()` → `tcp_local_ipv4_device()` | with `laddr == INADDR_ANY`, `SO_BINDTODEVICE` sets `conn->dev`; the option must be set *before* `bind()` |
| client source address | `tcp_send()` → `ipv4_build_header()` | TCP always writes `dev->d_ipaddr` as the source, so binding the device also picks the address |
| client egress | `devif_poll_tcp_connections()` | only polls connections whose `conn->dev == dev` |
| server device | `tcp_alloc_accept(dev, ...)` | the accepted connection takes the device the SYN arrived on (`eth1`) |
| server reply | `tcp_send()` | source `eth1`'s address, ARP for the client on `eth1`'s on-link subnet |

## What the program measures

- One direction (`-m tx`, the default), the reverse (`-m rx`), or full duplex
  (`-m both`) on one connection.
- Per-second rates on the **receiver's** count, so the number is bytes that
  actually crossed the cable and were read by the application.
- A payload check: each 32-bit word is its own index in the stream.  A
  mismatch is corruption, not a dropped packet; TCP would hide a drop.
- Stability: a broken connection is reopened, and a connection with no byte
  movement for 5 s is abandoned (TCP's own retransmission limit takes
  minutes).  Pulling the cable mid-run is a supported test.
- The summary gives the sustained average over the whole run, the min/max of
  the 1 s samples, the drop count and the mismatch count.

## Throughput caveats found while writing it

- **The board build is uniprocessor** (`CONFIG_SMP` off, `SMP_NCPUS=1`), so
  both endpoints, the stack, the driver and the payload check share one core.
- **A single connection is window-limited by its send buffer**
  (`CONFIG_NET_SEND_BUFSIZE`, 16 KiB here).  The program sets
  `SO_SNDBUF` to 32 KiB by default (`-w` changes it), but the receive window
  comes from the free IOBs, and the two NICs hold 48 IOBs of the 128 for their
  rings.  Raising `-w` too far starves the receive path, which shows as a
  *lower* rate.
- `-c` turns verification off for the cleanest rate number.

These are printed by the program rather than left to be guessed: the send
buffer and chunk size on the first connection, the per-direction counts and
the sample range at the end.

## Registration and build

Same pattern as `camenc`: the source is in the delivery repo, the build sees
it through `apps/examples/ethloop`, and the option lives in the defconfig.
Changing the defconfig requires `rm -rf cmake_out/contest2026_062_PharosTech_ethernet`
before `./build.sh ... --cmake`; the defconfig is not re-expanded otherwise.

`app/ethloop/CMakeLists.txt` and `Make.defs`/`Makefile` carry the same
application for the two build systems, and each says so.

## First run, and what it measured

30 s, `tx`, both ports 1000M/full: 488.9 MB received and verified, **0
mismatching words**, 0 drops, per-second rate 130.7–130.8 Mbit/s (±0.1%),
32 KiB still in flight when the connection was closed.

The path works.  The rate is the stack, not the wire: 16.3 MB/s with ~32 KiB
in flight implies a ~2 ms round trip, and the interface is idle between
windows.  A flat rate with no stalls or mismatches is what a clean cable and
a correct RGMII path look like; a marginal link would show retransmission
stalls (zero samples) rather than a lower steady number.  Levers: `-w`
(socket send buffer), `-m both`, and for a real number
`CONFIG_IOB_NBUFFERS`/`CONFIG_NET_SEND_BUFSIZE` (the 128-IOB pool holds 48
descriptors for the two rings, so the in-flight window is roughly the rest).

Two things the first run exposed and the code now handles:

- **The close at the deadline was a reset.**  The receiver side hit the
  deadline with unread data and `close()`d, sending RST, while the sender was
  still in `send()`: the log ended with `connection failed ... ENOTCONN`.
  Senders now `shutdown(SHUT_WR)` and receivers drain to the peer's FIN
  (bounded by a 3 s grace) before the socket is closed, and a failure that
  happens after the deadline is not reported as a broken connection.
- **Non-blocking `accept()` logged an ERROR every poll** (`si_accept failed:
  -11`), which interleaved with the application's buffered output and made
  the console look garbled.  The server now waits in `poll()` and calls
  `accept()` only when a connection is pending; stdout is line buffered.

## Status

and accept changes are built but not yet re-run.  For a long test, reflash

text:
我把三条都对照了源码、TRM、vendor DTB 和这次分支上已有的实测记录。结论是：**第 1、3 条成立，第 2 条的机制描述正确但前提（“MAC 不 snoop”）在这颗 SoC 上不成立**。逐条说依据。

---

## 1. link-down 直接 `goto rearm`：成立，是确定的缺陷

**代码路径核对**（[rk3576_gmac.c:2199](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L2199)）：

- [gm_phy_link()](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L877) 在 BMSR 的 link 位为 0 时返回 `OK` 且 `*up = false`。
- 2199 行的条件同时包含 `(ret == OK && !up)`，于是直接 [goto rearm](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L2227)。
- 结果是 [2260 行的 else 分支](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L2260)（`report = priv->carrier; priv->carrier = false;`）**永远走不到**——能绕过 2199 的只有 `ret > 0`，而 `gm_phy_link()` 从不返回正数。这是一段死代码，不是“有意不报 down”。

**后果**（与审查描述一致，且比它说的更彻底）：链接工作里**从不调用** `netdev_lower_carrier_off()`。于是 `IFF_RUNNING` 一直保持（[netdev_carrier.c:82](nuttx/net/netdev/netdev_carrier.c#L82)），`NETDEV_DOWN` / `arp_cleanup()` / `ip_frag_stop()` 都不会触发，`gmac0: link down` 这行日志永远打不出来；重插线时 `priv->carrier` 还是 true，`report = !priv->carrier` 为 false，也就没有 carrier-on。全驱动只有 `gm_ifdown()` 里会调 carrier_off，而那时 `priv->carrier` 已被置 true 后……顺序上只在 ifdown 才补发一次。

**修法**：只让 `ret == -EAGAIN` 提前返回，`OK && !up` 落到状态更新。有个坑要注意：现在 [2230 行的 `priv->trace_valid = false;`](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L2230) 之所以能保证“没插线时只打印一次 trace”，正是因为它只在 up 时执行；如果让 down 也落下来，必须把这一句挪进 `if (up)` 分支，否则每 1 秒会重打一次 trace。

**验证方法**：`ifup eth0` → 看到 `link up`，拔线应出现 `link down` 且 `ifconfig` 的 RUNNING 清掉；插回应再出现 `link up`。这一条与 ping 无关，不需要单次 ping 的限制。

---

## 2. RX 缓冲的 cache 交接：机制正确，但在 RK3576 上不是活 bug

审查对**机制的描述完全准确**，我逐点核实过：

- [gm_rx_arm_one()](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L1392) 在 `netpkt_alloc()` 后直接写 des0，只 [gm_desc_sync(desc)](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L1409) 清描述符，数据区没有任何维护；而 TX 方向是有的（[gm_buf_clean，1766 行](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L1766)）。这个不对称确实存在。
- 缓冲的脏行也确实会有：`iob_tryalloc()` 会把 `io_flink/io_len/io_offset/io_pktlen` 写一遍（[iob_alloc.c:137](nuttx/mm/iob/iob_alloc.c#L137)），`iob_free()` 又写 `io_flink`（[iob_free.c:176](nuttx/mm/iob/iob_free.c#L176)）。`struct iob_s` 的 `io_data` 只在 `base+16`，而 `io_data` 只保证 8 字节对齐；本镜像里 `g_iob_buffer` 在 `0x403e8eb0`，步长 1552，`io_data` 的行内偏移在 0/16/32/48 之间循环——**4 个缓冲里有 3 个，帧的起始 16–48 字节和 IOB 头共用一条 cache line**。
- 收包后的 [gm_buf_inval()](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L1835) 走到 [arm64_dcache_range()](nuttx/arch/arm64/src/common/arm64_cache.c#L142)，首条不对齐的行是 `dc civac`（[:153](nuttx/arch/arm64/src/common/arm64_cache.c#L153)）。如果这一行在交给 DMA 时是脏的，它会把旧的缓存内容写回，正好盖掉刚收到的帧头。

所以**若 MAC 真的不 snoop，后果不是“偶尔”，而是 3/4 的帧首行被确定性地写坏**——以太网头坏掉，TCP 根本不可能通。但事实上是通的：

- 本分支实测 30 s、`-m tx`、两端 1000M/full：**488.9 MB、0 个校验错、130.7–130.8 Mbit/s**（[ethloop.md](.dsh/memory/ethloop.md)）。TCP 能跑说明帧头是完好的。
- vendor DTB 的 gmac0/gmac1 节点都带 `dma-coherent`（[d.ts:4057](out/k7dtb/d_103642719.dts#L4057)、[:4123](out/k7dtb/d_103642719.dts#L4123)）。

## 3. 停止只等 RPS：成立，是拆解时的悬空风险

**核实**：

- [gm_mac_stop()](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L2143) 只轮询 `CH0STS_RPS`，超时后既不记录也不失败，函数还是 `void`。
- TX 侧的 `TPS`（CH0_STATUS bit 1）**在硬件头文件里根本没定义**（[rk3576_gmac.h:284](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/hardware/rk3576_gmac.h#L284) 只到 RPS）；TRM 里 TPS 明确存在（[Part2:155890](Rockchip_RK3576_TRM_Part2_V1.2_20240624.txt#L155890)）。
- [gm_ifdown()](contest2026_062_PharosTech/chips/rk3576/rk3576_gmac.c#L2526) 随后无条件调用 `gm_rings_free()`（它自己的注释还写着“The DMA must already be stopped”）。

**风险场景**：ifdown 时 TX 刚好在途。清 `ST` 只是“请求停止”，TPS 要等当前帧处理完才置位（1G 下一帧约 12 µs）；这段时间里 `gm_rings_free()` 已经把 `txpkt[]` 和 descriptor ring（`kmm_free`）释放了，DMA 若还在读就是 use-after-free。RX 侧 timeout 时同理。窗口小，但确实存在，属于 P2 而不是 P1。

**修法**按审查说的做，并补两个它没提的点：

- 头文件加 `RK3576_GMAC_CH0STS_TPS (1u << 1)`；
- 轮询前先把**陈旧的 RPS/TPS 清掉**（写 `CH0_STATUS` 的 W1C），否则上一次停止留下的位会让这次等待立刻“通过”（结尾的 `gm_putreg(STATUS, GM_IRQ_STATUS)` 也不含 TPS，清不掉它）；
- `gm_mac_stop()` 改返回 `int`，同时等 RPS|TPS，超时打印 status 并返回 `-ETIMEDOUT`；
- `gm_ifdown()` 只在成功时 `gm_rings_free()`。失败时保留内存（或先 `gm_reset()` 拉 CRU 复位再释放）。注意现在的顺序是“先置 `started=false`、拆中断，再 stop”，失败路径下端口会变成“栈认为 UP、驱动已死”的半死状态；要么把 stop 提到拆中断之前，要么失败时把 IRQ/started 恢复。

 *   The buffers live in the shared IOB pool and are not cache-line aligned:

 *   written back over the frame by that post-receive invalidate, and could
 *   also be evicted over it by unrelated cache traffic while the DMA owns the

  well as RPS (clearing both first, since they are write-1-to-clear),
  return -ETIMEDOUT, and on failure reset the port before releasing the
  rings -- or keep them.
- Guard receive/transmit/reclaim against running after ifdown has
  started, which a queued poll can do.

The GMAC is I/O-coherent on this part (TRM Part 1, CCI-500), so the
cache maintenance is defence rather than a live fix; it is kept
unconditional on purpose.

    interrupt enable does not gate, so the shared line stayed asserted and the

Now let me reconsider whether waiting for TPS could *always* time out on this hardware in a common case: When the TX engine is idle/suspended with no descriptors (TBU), is the "transmit process" in the stopped state or running? The TRM says TBU: "Transmission is suspended", i.e., the process is still active (ST=1). Clearing ST should stop it → TPS. Good.

But here's a potential gotcha: the DWC databook says "Transmit Process Stopped (TPS) — this bit is set when the transmission is stopped" and it's generated after the "stop" is complete. Some DWC versions require the TX FIFO to drain first, which could take up to the FIFO size at line rate (~130 µs for 16 KB at 1 Gbit/s). GM_RESET_TIMEOUT = 100 ms → enough.

What about the RX: clearing SR while the RX DMA is blocked on a full ring → RPS. Fine.

Another scenario: ifdown while the link is down. The DMA is running (ST/SR set) but no traffic; clearing ST/SR → TPS/RPS set quickly. Fine.

dump below is not cut off by a reset.
- NSH (priority 100) starved while the timer ISR runs means a task above it
  is spinning, most likely the network work queue (HPWORK, priority 192).

At 130.8 Mbit/s, 125 s is about 2.0 GB, within 6% of the 2^31-byte mark
where `conn->sent` / `isn + sent` cross the sign bit -- but NuttX's sequence
macros are the standard modulo form and should be safe there, so this is a
hypothesis, not a finding.

The diagnostic build (not yet run) adds:

- `rx <n> MB` and `iob <n free>` to every per-second line, so the last line
  before a wedge pins both the byte count and the pool state;
- `ethloop_monitor`, a pthread at priority **250** (above HPWORK) that wakes
  once a second and, after 6 s with no byte movement on an active
  connection, prints the counters and then `nxsched_foreach()` +
  `sched_dumpstack()` for every task.  The spin address maps against
  `cmake_out/<cfg>/System.map`.

If it wedges again, the dump says whether the spin is in `devif_poll` /
`tcp_send_buffered` / `netdev_upper_*` (stack) or in the driver, and whether
`iob` had reached zero.  The discriminating follow-up is
`ethloop -t 600 -w 65536`: a wedge at about twice the byte count in half the
wall time points at a byte-count boundary, a wedge at the same wall time at a
timer.

## The descriptor/cache-line race (the second failure, 64 KiB send buffer)

`ethloop -t 600 -w 65536` failed at once with `netdev_upper_txpoll: ERROR:
Transmit failed: -12` (ENOMEM, the driver's TX ring full) and the receiver
saw a trickle.  That is the fast reproducer for what the 1800 s run hits
after a few minutes.

The ring was packed at the hardware's 16-byte descriptor size, so four
descriptors share a 64-byte cache line, while `gm_desc_sync()` /
`gm_desc_inval()` work on lines.  Writing descriptor N+1 dirties the line
holding N and the following clean writes the whole line back -- including
N's cached OWN bit.  If the DMA completed N in between, the clean puts OWN=1
back; the DMA never revisits a descriptor behind the tail, so `gm_tx_reap()`
waits forever, the ring fills and every transmit returns -ENOMEM.  At a
steady 130 Mbit/s the window is small; a 64 KiB send buffer queues several
descriptors back to back and hits it at once.

Fix: one descriptor per cache line, with `DMA_CH0_CONTROL.DSL` telling the
DMA to skip the padding (`GM_DESC_STRIDE` 64, `GM_DESC_DSL` 6).  The skip is
in units of the data bus width, and the TRM gives this GMAC a 64-bit
application-side interface, so a unit is a dword (8 bytes) and
(64 - 16) / 8 = 6.  NuttX's STM32H7 driver does the same thing for its

the DMA walks 16-byte steps into the padding.

`txnow`/`txdone`/TX-IRQ count and every descriptor's OWN bit, and the app
prints the first five `send()` errnos and the per-second `rx MB` / `iob`

is 128-bit it would be 3) and whether this also removes the long-run wedge.

### Follow-up: the 64 KiB `-12` was the TX quota, not the ring

After the descriptor-stride change the 60 s run was clean, so DSL 6 is the
right unit.  `-w 65536` still failed at once.  The one-shot dump said:

```
gmac0: TX ring full txnow 5 txdone 6 txirqs 78 status 0x00000400
  txdesc[4] des3 0xb00005ea   (OWN=1, length 1514, in flight)
  every other des3 0x30000000 (OWN=0, FD|LD, completed)
```

So the ring was not stuck: six descriptors were complete and unreaped at that
instant, and TBU says the DMA had run out of work.  The real fault is the
quota: the ring keeps one of its eight slots empty to tell full from empty,
but `GM_TX_QUOTA` was the full eight.  A large send buffer makes the stack
offer eight packets in one poll; the eighth is refused with `-ENOMEM` after
TCP has already advanced past it, so the segment is lost and only an RTO
recovers it -- one drop per retransmission timeout, the 0.2 Mbit/s trickle in
the log.  `GM_TX_QUOTA` is now `GM_TX_DESC - 1`, so the stack stops before the
driver has to refuse.

The descriptor-stride change stays: four descriptors per cache line and a
line-wide clean really can put a completed neighbour's OWN bit back (the
`0x30000000` entries above show completions the driver had not reaped), even
if the 64 KiB symptom turned out to be the quota.  With the quota fixed the
driver should never see a full ring; the one-shot dump is still there in case
it does.

suspicion (the previous connection's `TIME_WAIT` expiring at 120 s) is dead.
The wedge always happens at `tx = 0x7AC8C000` (2,059,976,704 B), and
`2^32 - tx = 0x85374000` (2,234,990,592) is a plausible initial sequence
number, since NuttX picks one in [1e9, 3e9).  That makes the TCP sequence
wrap at 2^32 the leading explanation -- and it would repeat at the same byte
count on every boot only if this board's ARC4RNG hands out the same ISN each
time, which a fixed-seed boot would do.

`-R 60` did not avoid the wedge: it still stopped at the same cumulative
`tx = 0x7AC8C000` (~2.06 GB), now spread over three connections, so no
per-connection sequence or TIME_WAIT explanation survives.  The monitor's
